lines.text: In August 1945, one man survived the atomic bomb at Hiroshima. Three days later, he survived it again.
Tsutomu Yamaguchi, twenty-nine, designed oil tankers for Mitsubishi in Nagasaki.
That May, he was sent to Hiroshima for three months, leaving his wife and baby son behind.
August sixth was meant to be his last day there.
At eight fifteen, he saw a lone B-29 high above, and two small parachutes.
Then, in his words, a great flash in the sky, and he was blown over.
He was about three kilometres away. His face and arms were burned, an eardrum burst, and for a time he could not see.
By the end of the year, some one hundred and forty thousand people in Hiroshima would be dead.
He found his two colleagues, and they survived the night together.
The next day, they boarded a train home to Nagasaki.
On August ninth, wrapped in bandages, he went back to work.
He told his supervisor that one bomb had destroyed a whole city. His supervisor didn't believe him.
At eleven oh two, the same white light filled the room.
"I thought the mushroom cloud had followed me from Hiroshima."
Again, he was about three kilometres away, and again, he survived. So did his wife and son. Some seventy-four thousand people in Nagasaki did not.
After the war, he went back to designing ships, and for decades, rarely spoke about it.
In his eighties, he began telling his story, and in 2006, spoke at the United Nations against nuclear weapons.
In 2009, Japan officially recognised him as a survivor of both bombings, the only person ever to receive that status.
He hoped it would tell younger generations the horrifying history of the atomic bombings, even after he died.
Tsutomu Yamaguchi died in 2010, aged ninety-three.

Hook: bandaged Yamaguchi in the Nagasaki office, light swelling at the window
Nagasaki design office: drafting oil-tanker plans
May 1945: leaving wife and baby son at the door of the Nagasaki house
6 August, Hiroshima: streetcar stops, he walks toward the shipyard
He hears a plane, stops, looks up
POV: lone B-29 high above, two small parachutes
Flash: white light floods the street
Blast wave: dust wall, he is thrown down
Dust-darkened field: he rises, burned and deafened
Wide: the cloud over the flattened city
Night: three colleagues sit together amid the ruins
7 August: the evacuation train pulls out of the station
9 August, Nagasaki: bandaged, he walks to the shipyard office
He explains to his supervisor
The supervisor does not believe him
Wall clock: 11:02
The same white light fills the room
On the floor, looking toward the window: the quote
Cloud rising over Nagasaki's hills
Reunited with wife and son
The devastated Urakami valley, quiet
Years later: designing ships again, silent
2006: speaking at the United Nations
His hands holding the official recognition
Old Yamaguchi, the document on the table
Old Yamaguchi at the harbour at sunset
